findings.claim_checked_or_new: existing claim: nuclear 45Y/48E credits survive if construction begins before 2034, three-year phase-out after that
findings.what_you_found: Confirmed accurate against the enacted statute, not just the Morgan Lewis summary. 26 U.S.C. 45Y(d)(2)-(3) (as amended by OBBBA, Pub. L. 119-21) sets the 'applicable year' at calendar year 2032 for facilities other than wind and solar (this includes nuclear -- 45Y/48E are technology-neutral with wind/solar singled out for a separate, harsher rule). Facilities beginning construction in the first year following the applicable year (2033) get 100% of the credit; second year (2034) 75%; third year (2035) 50%; any later year 0%. So in plain terms: begin construction any time through the end of 2033 and the credit is undiminished; begin in 2034/2035 and it phases down; begin in 2036 or later and it's gone. This is exactly the 'before 2034, three-year phase-out' the site states (2033 inclusive = 'before 2034'). By contrast, wind and solar do NOT get a begin-construction phase-out at all -- OBBBA instead terminates their 45Y/48E credits outright for any facility placed in service after 2027, with a narrow carve-out only for projects that began construction by July 4, 2026. That is the real 'cliff-edge' deadline, and it applies to wind/solar, not nuclear.
findings.relevance_to_this_site: The site's headline claim holds up under primary-source scrutiny. Worth tightening the copy to state explicitly that nuclear's rule is begin-construction-based (not placed-in-service-based like wind/solar's), since that distinction is what makes 2033 a comfortable target for units the site tracks targeting 2028-2030 operation -- those projects need only start construction, not finish, before the deadline.

findings.claim_checked_or_new: resolving the conflicting secondary-source claim that nuclear faced a 'before December 31, 2028' cutoff
findings.what_you_found: That 2028 date is real but describes an EARLIER, non-enacted version of the bill, not current law. The House-passed draft (May 22, 2025) proposed a much more aggressive, accelerated sunset of nuclear credits; the Senate Finance Committee's June 16, 2025 draft separately proposed denying the credit to existing reactors using Russian- or Chinese-sourced fuel. Both were narrowed/replaced before the final bill was signed July 4, 2025. Any source still citing a 2028 nuclear construction deadline is describing a rejected draft. The enacted, currently-effective rule is the 2033/2034/2035 phase-out schedule in finding 'construction-deadline-confirmed' above.
findings.relevance_to_this_site: Confirms the site should NOT change its 2034 date. If anyone raises the 2028 figure (e.g. from an older secondary source), it can be corrected with this citation trail rather than treated as a live risk.

findings.claim_checked_or_new: new: does the FEOC 'material assistance' rule (Notice 2026-15) apply to nuclear the same as wind/solar, and what counts as material assistance
findings.what_you_found: Yes -- and this is the single most important update the site is missing detail on (it already has one bullet flagging FEOC as a 2026 risk, but with none of this mechanism). Treasury/IRS Notice 2026-15 (issued 2026-02-12) is the first guidance implementing 26 U.S.C. 45Y(b)(1)(E), the statutory provision (added by OBBBA) barring the credit for any Section 45Y or 48E qualified facility whose construction 'includes any material assistance from a prohibited foreign entity,' effective for construction beginning after December 31, 2025. The statute and the notice are both written generically ('any Section 45Y or 48E qualified facility') with no nuclear carve-out -- confirmed by multiple independent secondary summaries, none of which describe an exemption for nuclear. The notice sets up a Material Assistance Cost Ratio (MACR) test: (Total Direct Costs - PFE Direct Costs) / Total Direct Costs, and a facility fails (loses the credit) if that ratio falls below a statutory annual threshold for the year construction begins. A 'prohibited foreign entity' includes any government, agency, individual, or entity organized in or headquartered in Russia, China, Iran, or North Korea, or controlled by one ('foreign-influenced entity'). For a microreactor project, this means the DIRECT COSTS of TRISO fuel fabrication, enriched uranium (LEU or HALEU) feedstock/enrichment services, and reactor components sourced from a Russian- or Chinese-linked supplier would count against the MACR and could, above a certain proportion, disqualify the whole facility from the 45Y/48E credit -- directly relevant given Russia's (Rosatom/TENEX) dominant global enrichment position and China's growing HALEU ambitions. Important caveat: Treasury has NOT yet published the specific per-year MACR threshold table for electricity-generation facilities (the only concrete number found in secondary sources is a 2026 threshold of 55% for energy storage technologies, not generation facilities), and the notice explicitly defers full 'prohibited foreign entity' status determinations to future proposed regulations -- so exact compliance mechanics for a nuclear supply chain are still being worked out as of this writing (comment period closed 2026-03-30; interim rules apply until 60 days after final safe-harbor tables publish).
findings.relevance_to_this_site: This directly touches vendors already tracked on this site. Standard Nuclear and BWXT TRISO fuel supply deals should be checked for where their fuel/enrichment inputs originate -- a deal reliant on Russian-enriched uranium (even indirectly, via feedstock) could jeopardize a customer's 45Y/48E eligibility even if the customer's own construction-start date clears the 2033 deadline easily. The site's current single bullet ('New risk: [...] material-assistance thresholds on the supply chain that a HALEU/TRISO vendor has to clear to keep the credit') is directionally correct but underspecified -- it doesn't name the effective date (construction beginning after 12/31/2025), the covered countries (Russia/China/Iran/North Korea), or that the specific threshold numbers for generation facilities are not yet public. Recommend costs.json be updated (in a separate pass) to add these specifics and this notice as a second source.

findings.claim_checked_or_new: new: does the FEOC material-assistance rule apply to Section 45U (existing-fleet credit) the same way it applies to 45Y/48E (new-build)
findings.what_you_found: No -- and this is a distinction the site should preserve if it ever discusses 45U. Section 45U (Zero-Emission Nuclear PTC, for reactors placed in service before Aug 16, 2022 -- not relevant to this site's new-build microreactor tracker, but worth getting right if referenced) is subject to the basic FEOC restrictions (specified foreign entities cannot claim it at all as of enactment; foreign-influenced entities lose eligibility for tax years beginning after the second anniversary of enactment; and after Dec 31, 2027 taxpayers must certify nuclear fuel wasn't sourced from a covered nation/entity, grandfathering binding contracts in force before Jan 1, 2023). But per Morgan Lewis's own July 2025 article -- read in full, not just the FEOC bullet the site currently cites -- 45U is explicitly carved OUT of the harsher 'effective control' and 'material assistance' (MACR) provisions that apply to 45Y/48E. That MACR/cost-ratio mechanism is what Notice 2026-15 implements, and it is a 45Y/48E-and-45X-specific test.
findings.relevance_to_this_site: Not directly relevant to the site's new-build microreactor deployments (which claim 45Y/48E, not 45U), but important if any future content conflates the two credits' FEOC exposure -- 45Y/48E-claiming microreactor projects face the full MACR supply-chain test described above; an existing large reactor claiming 45U faces a lighter-touch fuel-sourcing certification only.

findings.claim_checked_or_new: new: has Section 45J (advanced nuclear PTC, already claimed by Vogtle) changed
findings.what_you_found: No material OBBBA-era change surfaced for Section 45J specifically. findings.claim_checked_or_new: new: does IRS's 'beginning of construction' test (5% safe harbor vs. physical work test) apply identically to nuclear as to wind/solar, especially after the Aug 2025 revision
findings.what_you_found: The August 15, 2025 Notice 2025-42 revision -- which eliminated the 5% safe harbor for most wind and solar projects (limiting it to solar facilities of 1.5 MW AC or less) and pushed those technologies toward the physical-work test as the primary route -- applies ONLY to wind and solar. Multiple independent secondary summaries state this explicitly: other Section 45Y/48E technologies, nuclear included, are unaffected by Notice 2025-42 and remain governed by the prior beginning-of-construction guidance (the traditional line of IRS notices, e.g. the framework originating in Notice 2013-29 and its successors, which offers both the 5% safe harbor and the physical work test as alternative routes). So for the microreactor projects this site tracks (Aalo, Antares, BWXT BANR, Oklo, Radiant, Valar, Westinghouse eVinci, X-energy), once any of them announces a formal construction start, they can establish it either by incurring 5%+ of total project cost (the safe harbor) or by beginning physical work of a significant nature on-site or on custom-fabricated equipment off-site (the physical work test) -- whichever is administratively easier -- unlike wind/solar developers who, post-Sept 2, 2025, mostly cannot rely on the cost-based safe harbor at all.
findings.relevance_to_this_site: Useful operational detail if the site ever adds a per-project 'construction start' tracking field: nuclear projects have more flexibility (both safe-harbor routes) than wind/solar in establishing a qualifying start date, which somewhat de-risks the 2033 deadline for projects that slip on physical construction but can still satisfy the 5% cost safe harbor early. None of the 8 tracked deployments have disclosed a formal IRS-qualifying construction-start date as of this pass -- this remains, as the site already says, 'an open item per project.'
